content: Brassica is a genus of plants that belongs to the mustard family, scientifically known as Brassicaceae. The plants within this genus are commonly referred to as cabbages or mustards. Certain crops derived from this genus are also collectively called cole crops. This genus is particularly notable for including a greater number of agriculturally and horticulturally significant crops than any other genus. Additionally, it encompasses various weed species, which include both wild taxa and plants that have escaped from cultivation. The genus Brassica consists of over 30 wild species and hybrids, along with numerous cultivated varieties and hybrids of domesticated origin. Most species within this genus are annual or biennial plants, although some are small shrubs. Geographically, Brassica species are native to the wild regions of western Europe, the Mediterranean, and temperate areas of Asia. While cultivated species are grown globally, many wild species have adapted to grow as weeds, particularly in regions such as North America, South America, and Australia. Various parts of Brassica plants have been selectively developed for human consumption. These include the roots (e.g., swedes and turnips), stems (e.g., kohlrabi), leaves (e.g., cabbage and Brussels sprouts), flowers (e.g., cauliflower and broccoli), and seeds (e.g., mustard seeds and oilseed rape). Some forms of Brassica with white or purple foliage or flower heads are also cultivated for ornamental purposes. Furthermore, Brassica species serve as food sources for the larvae of several Lepidoptera species, as detailed in the list of Lepidoptera that feed on Brassica. Due to their significant agricultural value, Brassica plants have been the focus of extensive scientific research. The close genetic relationships among six economically important species—Brassica carinata, B. juncea, B. oleracea, B. napus, B. nigra, and B. rapa—are explained by the Triangle of U theory. Brassica vegetables are highly esteemed for their nutritional benefits, as they are rich in vitamin C and soluble fiber. They also contain several bioactive compounds with potent anti-cancer properties, such as 3,3'-diindolylmethane, sulforaphane, and selenium. Recent research conducted at the University of California, Berkeley, has revealed that 3,3'-diindolylmethane found in Brassica vegetables is a powerful modulator of the innate immune response, exhibiting strong antiviral, antibacterial, and anti-cancer activities. There is some disagreement among botanists regarding the classification and status of Brassica species and subspecies. However, the following list highlights some of the economically significant species: Brassica carinata: Known as Abyssinian mustard or Abyssinian cabbage, it is used for biodiesel production. Brassica elongata: Commonly referred to as elongated mustard. Brassica fruticulosa: Also called Mediterranean cabbage. Brassica juncea: Includes Indian mustard, brown mustard, leaf mustards, and Sarepta mustard. Brassica napus: Encompasses rapeseed, canola, rutabaga (Swede turnip), and nabicol. Brassica narinosa: Known as broadbeaked mustard. Brassica nigra: Commonly referred to as black mustard. Brassica oleracea: Includes kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kai-lan, and Brussels sprouts. Brassica perviridis: Known as tender green or mustard spinach. Brassica rapa (synonym: Brassica campestris): Includes Chinese cabbage, turnip, rapini, mustard, and komatsuna. Brassica rupestris: Known as brown mustard. Brassica septiceps: Commonly referred to as seven-top turnip. Brassica tournefortii: Known as Asian mustard. Some species names have been deprecated. For example, Brassica kaber (wild mustard or charlock) is now classified as Sinapis arvensis, and Brassica alba or Brassica hirta (white or yellow mustard) is now classified as Sinapis alba. In terms of genetics, the genome of Brassica rapa is currently being sequenced by an international consortium. This genome represents the A genome component of the amphidiploid crop species Brassica napus and Brassica juncea.
